# Benzaiten walks into a finance, wealth & commerce firm

Somewhere right now, in a finance, wealth & commerce office, someone is doing exactly what the myths describe — and has never heard of **Benzaiten**. This file is the introduction.

## Before the Office, the Story

**The River Who Became Speech.** In India, Sarasvatī was first a river and then a goddess.  The Ṛgveda (6. 61) hymns her in the triple superlative: 'the best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses,' flowing mountain-strong from the heights to the sea.

**The Goddess Who Guards the Preachers.** Buddhism carried Sarasvatī east, and the Lotus Sūtra gave her its highest commission.  In the chapter devoted to her, she appears before the assembly with her retinue and vows to protect and nourish all who keep, recite, and preach the sūtra in the 'evil age to come': she will grant them eloquence, memory, and 'the charm of voice' that can win every assembly, and she teaches a dhāraṇī for their safety.  The commission is the pivot of her whole biography: the river-goddess who once watered fields becomes the guardian of the text-field — the first link in the chain that ends, centuries later, in a Japanese fortune ship.

## The Reveal, Seat by Seat

### Finance, Wealth & Commerce

*Wealth, fortune, and commercial luck; her biwa plays the sound of money.* The match is not poetic license. Strip the trade to its function and the function is the myth.

### Music, Arts & Performance

Now read the why-line with the office in mind: *The only female among the Seven Lucky Gods, patron of music, song, and the biwa.* The people doing this work did not borrow the archetype. They re-derived it — the way Benzaiten was always going to be re-derived wherever music, wealth, eloquence matters.

### Writing, Publishing & Media

*Goddess of eloquence; the word made persuasive is her instrument.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

## Not the First Rebrand

Benzaiten is a palimpsest in three scripts.  The underlayer is Indian: Sarasvatī, the Vedic river who became the goddess of speech, carried into Buddhism and east along the caravan roads. The office is only the latest translation.
